newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat chairman goes on trial for fraud.
newsitem.headline: Fiat chairman goes on trial for fraud.

text.p: The chairman of Italian car corporation Fiat, Cesare Romiti, went on trial on Wednesday on charges of accounting fraud and making illegal payments to politicians and managers working overseas.

The hearing was formally opened after 150 workers at Fiat, a group of trades unionists and left-wing sympathisers and a single shareholder lodged separate requests to present themselves as civil plaintiffs at the trial.
The trial in Turin, where Fiat has its headquarters, was later adjourned until Thursday to give defence lawyers time to decide whether they could legally challenge the requests.
Also on trial with Romiti is Fiat's finance director, Francesco Paolo Mattioli. The two men face similar charges, although Romiti is also being tried on a count of tax fraud.
Romiti took over the running of Italy's largest industrial group last March when Gianni Agnelli stood down after more than 30 years at the helm.

The two top managers are accused of diverting more than 30 billion lire ($19.8 million) into overseas accounts from the 1980s. Prosecutors allege the funds were used to make payments to political parties, politicians and Fiat managers abroad.
The hearing is being conducted behind closed doors under a fast-track, plea-bargaining procedure in which the defendants would receive a reduced sentence if convicted.
The procedure, which can result in any jail sentence being suspended, does not require defendants to plead guilty.
The party of Fiat workers, who gathered in front of the court building, believe that the alleged accounting fraud had an impact on their pay, a lawyer acting on their behalf said.

Romiti's lawyer, Vittorio Chiusano, told reporters: "We cannot let this trial turn into a political gathering. The presence of these workers is a means of forcing the situation and generating emotions around the trial."

Romiti and Mattioli are the first top executives at the company to face criminal proceedings since Fiat's founder Giovanni Agnelli, grandfather of Gianni Agnelli, stood trial on charges of falsifying accounts in 1912. He was acquitted.
